newsitem.title: USA: U.S. sees economy, Russian role as G7 summit focus.
newsitem.headline: U.S. sees economy, Russian role as G7 summit focus.

text.p: This week's G7 summit in Denver will showcase the strength of the U.S. economy as well as Russia's growing, though incomplete, integration into the West's major institutions, U.S. officials said on Monday.

The June 20-22 summit will gather leaders of the Group of Seven (G7) -- Britain, Canada, France, Germany, Italy, and the United States -- along with Russian President Boris Yeltsin for a discussion of global economic and political problems.

Basking in the robust health of its economy, the United States may have the luxury of lecturing its allies about taking structural reforms, like cutting budget deficits and reining in social spending, to create jobs.

If it cannot resist the temptation to do so, it will have turned the tables from the 1993 Tokyo meeting, when President Bill Clinton was taken to task at his first G7 summit for the ballooning U.S. deficit and its threat to the world economy.

"In 1993, the U.S. budget deficit was really the central economic concern of the summit," White House aide Daniel Tarullo said. "Today, the stellar performance of the U.S. economy will be the principal focus of economic attention."

According to the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development (OECD), the United States will have unemployment of 5.0 percent this year, growth of 3.6 percent and a budget deficit of just 1.1 percent of its gross domestic product.

In contrast, the economies of France, Germany and Italy are all sluggish and suffer from double-digit unemployment. All three are forecast by the OECD this year to have identical 3.2 percent budget-deficit-to-GDP ratios.
Asked if he expected Europe's slack growth to come up at Denver, Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin replied: "Oh yes."

"Europe is going through a very difficult period," he added. "I have no doubt that we will have discussions, as we always do, about the structural issues that impede economic activity in Europe, particularly impede job growth."

The Europeans themselves are at loggerheads over their plans for Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), with France's newly-elected socialist government reluctant to commit to further austerity to meet the criteria for a single currency.

European Union finance ministers meeting in Amsterdam on Monday drafted a resolution on economic growth and employment that assuaged France's concerns that the bloc was excessively focused on fiscal austerity.
The resolution, if approved by EU leaders, appeared likely to paper over the dispute but U.S. officials said they still expected EMU to come up on the sidelines of the Denver summit.
Another contentious topic that will be broached outside the summit's formal meetings is the eastward expansion of the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation.
Defying its allies, the United States wants to invite only three nations -- Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic -- to begin negotiations to enter the western security alliance.
France and Germany on Friday insisted they would support Romania and Slovenia for membership despite the U.S. stance.
U.S. officials said Clinton expected to raise the issue in bilateral meetings on Friday in Denver with French President Jacques Chirac and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi.
Clinton is also scheduled to hold a bilateral meeting with Yeltsin on Friday, before the summit's formal start, that will touch on arms control and Russia's economic reform.
To reflect Russia's expanded role at the Denver meeting, the United States has dubbed it the "Summit of the Eight."
